sections.title: Doctrine

sentences.text: The President's executive power is not limited to those specifically enumerated in the Constitution but includes residual powers necessary to protect the general welfare of the people and preserve the State.
This residual power is founded on the President's duty as steward of the people and protector of the peace, allowing action not forbidden by the Constitution or laws that the nation's needs demand.

While the right to return to one's country is a distinct right under international law and part of the law of the land, it is not absolute and may be restricted if it poses a serious threat to national interest and welfare.

Judicial power, under the 1987 Constitution, includes the duty to determine whether there has been grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any government branch, thereby limiting the political question doctrine and allowing courts to inquire into the factual bases of executive decisions.

sections.title: Facts

sentences.text: In February 1986, Ferdinand E. Marcos was deposed from the presidency through a non-violent "people power" revolution and forced into exile.
Corazon C. Aquino was subsequently declared President under a revolutionary government, and her presidency was reinforced by the ratification of the 1987 Constitution.

Despite this, the Aquino government faced numerous challenges, including the failed Manila Hotel coup in 1986, the takeover of television station Channel 7 by rebel troops with "Marcos loyalists" support, and an unsuccessful plot by the Marcos spouses to return from Hawaii with mercenaries.

Other significant threats included a failed coup on August 28, 1987, led by Col. Gregorio Honasan, communist insurgency, and a secessionist movement in Mindanao, all of which contributed to political instability.

Economically, the nation was devastated by accumulated foreign debt and alleged plunder attributed to Mr. Marcos and his cronies, with efforts at recovery and retrieval of ill-gotten wealth remaining elusive.
Mr. Marcos, in his deathbed, expressed a wish to return to the Philippines to die.
However, President Aquino firmly decided to bar the return of Mr. Marcos and his family, citing dire consequences to the nation's stability and economy.

Consequently, Ferdinand E. Marcos, Imelda R. Marcos, Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr., Irene M. Araneta, Imee Manotoc, Tomas Manotoc, Gregorio Araneta, Pacifico E. Marcos, Nicanor Yñiguez, and the Philippine Constitution Association (PHILCONSA) filed a petition for mandamus and prohibition.
The petitioners sought an order for respondents to issue travel documents to Mr. Marcos and his immediate family and to enjoin the implementation of the President's decision to bar their return.

sections.title: Petitioners’ arguments

sentences.text: The petitioners assert that the President lacks the power to impair the liberty of abode and the right to travel of the Marcoses, as these rights are guaranteed under Section 1 and Section 6 of the Bill of Rights.

The petitioners contend that the President cannot impair their liberty of abode because only a court may do so "within the limits prescribed by law," and the right to travel cannot be impaired because no law has authorized it, arguing that legislation is required for such impairment.
The petitioners advance the view that the President's powers are limited to those specifically enumerated in the 1987 Constitution, asserting that what is not enumerated is impliedly denied.

sections.title: Respondents’ arguments

sentences.text: The respondents' principal argument is that the issue involves a political question, which is non-justiciable, as it concerns the President's determination that the Marcoses' return would endanger national security and public safety.

The respondents argue for the primacy of the State's right to national security over individual rights, citing Article II, Section 4 and Section 5 of the Constitution, which state that the government's prime duty is to serve and protect the people and that maintaining peace and order is essential for the enjoyment of democracy.

The decision to ban the Marcos family for national security reasons has international precedents, citing cases of other deposed dictators whose return to their homelands was prevented by their governments.

sections.title: Issue

sentences.text: May the President, in the exercise of constitutional powers, prohibit Ferdinand E. Marcos and his family from returning to the Philippines?
Is the President's power to bar the Marcoses' return a political question?
Does the President have the power to bar the return of former President Marcos and his family to the Philippines?

Did the President act arbitrarily or with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction in determining that the return of the Marcoses poses a serious threat to national interest and welfare and in prohibiting their return?

sections.text:
May the President, in the exercise of constitutional powers, prohibit Ferdinand E. Marcos and his family from returning to the Philippines?

# Sub-issues:
- Is the President's power to bar the Marcoses' return a political question?
- Does the President have the power to bar the return of former President Marcos and his family to the Philippines?
- Did the President act arbitrarily or with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction in determining that the return of the Marcoses poses a serious threat to national interest and welfare and in prohibiting their return?

sections.title: Ruling

sentences.text: No, the President did not act arbitrarily or with grave abuse of discretion in determining that the return of former President Marcos and his family at the present time and under present circumstances poses a serious threat to national interest and welfare and in prohibiting their return to the Philippines.
The instant petition is hereby DISMISSED.
Chief Justice Fernan also concurred, while Justices Gutierrez, Jr., Cruz, Paras, Padilla, and Sarmiento dissented.

sections.title: Ratio Decidendi

blocks.heading: 1. The right involved is the right to return to one's country, distinct from the right to travel.

sentences.text: The Court clarified that the individual right at issue is the right to return to one's country, which is a distinct right under international law, separate from the liberty of abode or the right to travel within or out of the Philippines.
This right to return is considered a generally accepted principle of international law and, under the Constitution, is part of the law of the land, protected against arbitrary deprivation.
Therefore, the limitations on the right to return are not necessarily the same as those for the liberty of abode and the right to travel.

blocks.heading: 2. The President possesses residual executive powers to protect the general welfare and national interest.

sentences.text: The 1987 Constitution vests executive power in the President but does not exhaustively define it.

The Court held that "executive power" is more than the sum of specific enumerated powers, maintaining intact what is traditionally considered within its scope, and includes the President's residual power to protect the general welfare of the people.

The President, as protector of the peace, has wide discretion to attend to day-to-day problems of maintaining peace and order and ensuring domestic tranquility, and can take pre-emptive action against threats to the State's existence.

blocks.heading: 3. The Court can review executive actions for grave abuse of discretion, limiting the political question doctrine.

sentences.text: The Court rejected the Solicitor General's argument that the issue was a political question beyond judicial review.

Under Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, judicial power includes the duty to determine whether there has been grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any government branch.

The Constitution limits resort to the political question doctrine and broadens the scope of judicial inquiry, empowering the Court to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion and to ascertain if the Executive has gone beyond constitutional limits.
The Court's function is to check, not to supplant, the Executive, and to determine if factual bases exist for the President's conclusion.

blocks.heading: 4. Factual bases exist for the President's decision to bar the Marcoses' return.

sentences.text: Based on pleadings, oral arguments, and a briefing by the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces and the National Security Adviser, the Court found factual bases for the President's decision.
The Court acknowledged the ongoing threats from a well-organized communist insurgency, a separatist movement in Mindanao, rightist conspiracies, and urban terrorism.
The documented history of the Marcoses' and their followers' efforts to destabilize the country supported the conclusion that their return would exacerbate violence and instigate chaos.

The President's determination that the Marcoses' return posed a serious threat to national interest and welfare was not arbitrary or capricious, especially considering the potential "catalytic effect" on various destabilizing forces.
Furthermore, the country was still recovering from economic hardships attributed to the Marcos regime, and their return could wipe away gains and lead to total economic collapse.

This right to return is considered a generally accepted principle of international law and, under the Constitution, is part of the law of the land, protected against arbitrary deprivation. Therefore, the limitations on the right to return are not necessarily the same as those for the liberty of abode and the right to travel.

# 2. The President possesses residual executive powers to protect the general welfare and national interest.
The 1987 Constitution vests executive power in the President but does not exhaustively define it. The Court held that "executive power" is more than the sum of specific enumerated powers, maintaining intact what is traditionally considered within its scope, and includes the President's residual power to protect the general welfare of the people. The President, as protector of the peace, has wide discretion to attend to day-to-day problems of maintaining peace and order and ensuring domestic tranquility, and can take pre-emptive action against threats to the State's existence.

# 3. The Court can review executive actions for grave abuse of discretion, limiting the political question doctrine.
The Court rejected the Solicitor General's argument that the issue was a political question beyond judicial review. Under Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, judicial power includes the duty to determine whether there has been grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any government branch. The Constitution limits resort to the political question doctrine and broadens the scope of judicial inquiry, empowering the Court to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion and to ascertain if the Executive has gone beyond constitutional limits. The Court's function is to check, not to supplant, the Executive, and to determine if factual bases exist for the President's conclusion.

# 4. Factual bases exist for the President's decision to bar the Marcoses' return.
Based on pleadings, oral arguments, and a briefing by the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces and the National Security Adviser, the Court found factual bases for the President's decision. The Court acknowledged the ongoing threats from a well-organized communist insurgency, a separatist movement in Mindanao, rightist conspiracies, and urban terrorism. The documented history of the Marcoses' and their followers' efforts to destabilize the country supported the conclusion that their return would exacerbate violence and instigate chaos. The President's determination that the Marcoses' return posed a serious threat to national interest and welfare was not arbitrary or capricious, especially considering the potential "catalytic effect" on various destabilizing forces. Furthermore, the country was still recovering from economic hardships attributed to the Marcos regime, and their return could wipe away gains and lead to total economic collapse.

sections.title: The Dissents (useful for recitation)

sentences.text: Justice Gutierrez, Jr. argued that the issue is one of rights, not power, and that the Court should not interpret the Constitution for only one person, as this smacks of unequal protection.
He contended that Section 6 of the Bill of Rights requires a *law* to impair the liberty of abode or the right to travel, and no such law exists to justify the ban.

He criticized the application of the political question doctrine, noting that the 1987 Constitution's expanded definition of judicial power (Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2) was specifically enacted to prevent the Court from avoiding controversial decisions.
He found no textual constitutional commitment of the issue solely to the President and no unmanageable standards for judicial determination.

The military briefing did not establish a "clear and present danger" related to Mr. Marcos, and the President's stated reasons of "national welfare and interest" or "preserving economic and political gains" are too generic to override a constitutional right.
He warned against the "confluence theory" or "catalytic effect" as a dangerous precedent for denying civil liberties.
He concluded that the government has ample powers to deal with a person who transgresses the peace, but denying travel papers is not one of them, as there is no law prescribing exile as a penalty.
Justice Cruz believed that Ferdinand Marcos, as a Filipino citizen, is entitled to return to and die in his own country, regardless of his past actions.
He stated that the fears expressed by government representatives during the closed-door briefing were based on mere conjectures without concrete evidence.
He criticized the majority for reinstating the "residual powers" doctrine, which he saw as a step backward and contrary to the Constitutional Commission's intent to limit presidential powers.
He emphasized that judicial decisions should be based on established facts and applicable law, not personal feelings, prejudice, or fear.
He asserted that the constitutional rights to travel and liberty of abode apply to all individuals, including tyrants and scoundrels, just as they applied to Benigno Aquino, Jr.
Justice Paras dissented, questioning whether the nation was ready to be called a society without compassion.

He agreed that Marcos, as a Filipino citizen, has the right to return to his country under both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the 1987 Constitution, unless national safety and security demand otherwise.
However, he found that the Armed Forces failed to prove this danger, relying on speculation rather than hard evidence.
He found it incredible that one man and his family, ousted by popular will, could arouse an entire country to morbid sympathy.
He suggested allowing Marcos to return under conditions of house arrest in Ilocos Norte, with burial restrictions, to maintain regard for human rights, national discipline, and compassion.

Justice Padilla viewed the core issue as a justiciable conflict between a Filipino's right to return and the government's power to bar it in the interest of national security and public safety, emphasizing the expanded judicial review under the 1987 Constitution.

He argued that the right to travel includes the right to return to the country and that while the State can restrict travel based on police power even without specific legislation, such power cannot be arbitrary or irrational.

He found that the respondents failed to present sufficient convincing evidence to justify negating Marcos's right to return, stating that their apprehensions were more speculative than real and could be controlled by the government.

He stressed that deteriorating conditions should not be a pretext for derogating human rights and that the Philippines, as a UN member, must adhere to international law guaranteeing the right to return.
He rejected the political question argument, asserting that the Court has a clear duty to uphold specific constitutional and human rights against simplistic generalities.
He drew a parallel to the denial of Benigno S. Aquino, Jr.'s right to return in 1983, suggesting that the mistake should not be repeated.
Justice Sarmiento argued that the President's implied powers must yield to the paramountcy of the Bill of Rights.
He contended that the Constitution explicitly states that the right to travel can only be impaired by a decree of statute or a lawful judicial mandate, and not by presidential action.
He noted that the 1987 Constitution divested the Executive of the implied power to moderate citizen movement, unlike the 1973 Constitution.
He questioned the factual basis for the alleged threat, pointing out that military officials stated the government would not fall if Marcos returned, contradicting the claims of national danger.
He criticized the majority's reliance on "residual power" and the President's role as "protector of peace" as reminiscent of justifications for authoritarian rule under the martial law regime.

Despite personal suffering under the Marcos regime, including the death of his son and his own arrest, he maintained that Marcos's constitutional right to return should be upheld, emphasizing that human rights violations should not be repeated against anyone.

# Gutierrez, Jr., J., dissenting
Justice Gutierrez, Jr. argued that the issue is one of rights, not power, and that the Court should not interpret the Constitution for only one person, as this smacks of unequal protection. He contended that Section 6 of the Bill of Rights requires a *law* to impair the liberty of abode or the right to travel, and no such law exists to justify the ban. He criticized the application of the political question doctrine, noting that the 1987 Constitution's expanded definition of judicial power (Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2) was specifically enacted to prevent the Court from avoiding controversial decisions. He found no textual constitutional commitment of the issue solely to the President and no unmanageable standards for judicial determination. The military briefing did not establish a "clear and present danger" related to Mr. Marcos, and the President's stated reasons of "national welfare and interest" or "preserving economic and political gains" are too generic to override a constitutional right. He warned against the "confluence theory" or "catalytic effect" as a dangerous precedent for denying civil liberties. He concluded that the government has ample powers to deal with a person who transgresses the peace, but denying travel papers is not one of them, as there is no law prescribing exile as a penalty.

# Cruz, J., dissenting
Justice Cruz believed that Ferdinand Marcos, as a Filipino citizen, is entitled to return to and die in his own country, regardless of his past actions. He stated that the fears expressed by government representatives during the closed-door briefing were based on mere conjectures without concrete evidence. He criticized the majority for reinstating the "residual powers" doctrine, which he saw as a step backward and contrary to the Constitutional Commission's intent to limit presidential powers. He emphasized that judicial decisions should be based on established facts and applicable law, not personal feelings, prejudice, or fear. He asserted that the constitutional rights to travel and liberty of abode apply to all individuals, including tyrants and scoundrels, just as they applied to Benigno Aquino, Jr.

# Paras, J., dissenting
Justice Paras dissented, questioning whether the nation was ready to be called a society without compassion. He agreed that Marcos, as a Filipino citizen, has the right to return to his country under both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the 1987 Constitution, unless national safety and security demand otherwise. However, he found that the Armed Forces failed to prove this danger, relying on speculation rather than hard evidence. He found it incredible that one man and his family, ousted by popular will, could arouse an entire country to morbid sympathy. He suggested allowing Marcos to return under conditions of house arrest in Ilocos Norte, with burial restrictions, to maintain regard for human rights, national discipline, and compassion.

# Padilla, J., dissenting
Justice Padilla viewed the core issue as a justiciable conflict between a Filipino's right to return and the government's power to bar it in the interest of national security and public safety, emphasizing the expanded judicial review under the 1987 Constitution. He argued that the right to travel includes the right to return to the country and that while the State can restrict travel based on police power even without specific legislation, such power cannot be arbitrary or irrational. He found that the respondents failed to present sufficient convincing evidence to justify negating Marcos's right to return, stating that their apprehensions were more speculative than real and could be controlled by the government. He stressed that deteriorating conditions should not be a pretext for derogating human rights and that the Philippines, as a UN member, must adhere to international law guaranteeing the right to return. He rejected the political question argument, asserting that the Court has a clear duty to uphold specific constitutional and human rights against simplistic generalities. He drew a parallel to the denial of Benigno S. Aquino, Jr.'s right to return in 1983, suggesting that the mistake should not be repeated.

# Sarmiento, J., dissenting
Justice Sarmiento argued that the President's implied powers must yield to the paramountcy of the Bill of Rights. He contended that the Constitution explicitly states that the right to travel can only be impaired by a decree of statute or a lawful judicial mandate, and not by presidential action. He noted that the 1987 Constitution divested the Executive of the implied power to moderate citizen movement, unlike the 1973 Constitution. He questioned the factual basis for the alleged threat, pointing out that military officials stated the government would not fall if Marcos returned, contradicting the claims of national danger. He criticized the majority's reliance on "residual power" and the President's role as "protector of peace" as reminiscent of justifications for authoritarian rule under the martial law regime. Despite personal suffering under the Marcos regime, including the death of his son and his own arrest, he maintained that Marcos's constitutional right to return should be upheld, emphasizing that human rights violations should not be repeated against anyone.

sections.title: Topic Explained

blocks.heading: 1. Executive Power: Enumerated vs. Residual Powers

sentences.text: The case of Marcos v. Manglapus delves into the nature and scope of "executive power" under the Philippine Constitution.

While the Constitution enumerates specific powers of the President (e.g., control over executive departments, commander-in-chief powers, pardoning power), it does not explicitly define "executive power."

The Court held that executive power is not limited to the enumerated powers but includes the President's residual power to protect the general welfare of the people, which is inherent in the President's role as head of state and government.
These residual powers are derived from the President's fundamental duty to serve and protect the people, maintain peace and order, promote general welfare, and preserve and defend the Constitution.
This means the President can take actions not explicitly forbidden by law or the Constitution if the needs of the nation demand it, particularly in safeguarding national security and public interest.

blocks.heading: 2. The Political Question Doctrine and Judicial Review

sentences.text: Traditionally, the political question doctrine holds that certain issues are beyond the judiciary's scope because they are committed to the discretion of the political branches (Executive or Legislative) or lack judicially manageable standards.
However, the 1987 Philippine Constitution significantly modified this doctrine.

Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2, explicitly states that judicial power includes the duty to determine whether there has been a "grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government."
This provision allows the Supreme Court to review actions of the Executive, even those involving national security, to ensure that the President has not acted arbitrarily or capriciously.
The Court's role is to check, not to supplant, the Executive, by examining if factual bases exist for the President's decision.

blocks.heading: 3. Right to Return to One's Country vs. Right to Travel

sentences.text: The case distinguishes between the general "right to travel" (within the country or to other countries) and the specific "right to return to one's country."

While the Bill of Rights (Article III, Section 6) guarantees the liberty of abode and the right to travel, subject to impairment "as may be provided by law" in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health, the right to return is treated differently.

The right to return is recognized as a generally accepted principle of international law, enshrined in instruments like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and is considered part of the law of the land.
Under international law, this right is protected against "arbitrary deprivation."

This case demonstrates that even this fundamental right can be restricted when it poses a serious threat to national interest and welfare, as determined by the President, subject to judicial review for grave abuse of discretion.

sections.title: Why This Case Matters

sentences.text: This case is crucial for understanding the expansive nature of "executive power" in the Philippines, establishing that the President possesses residual powers beyond those explicitly enumerated in the Constitution, particularly in matters of national security and welfare.

It redefines the political question doctrine under the 1987 Constitution, clarifying that the Supreme Court can now inquire into whether the Executive has gravely abused its discretion, even in sensitive areas like national security, by examining the factual bases of the President's decisions.

The decision distinguishes the "right to return to one's country" from the general "right to travel," recognizing the former as a distinct right under international law that is part of the law of the land, but also affirming that it is not absolute and can be restricted under compelling circumstances.

The case highlights the balance between individual constitutional rights and the State's paramount duty to protect its people and ensure national security and stability, considering the profound effect on national life, the devastated economy, and threats to government stability.
